items.stem: Which of the following is an output from a drainage basin system?
items.answer: Evapotranspiration
items.markingKey: B. Outputs are evaporation, transpiration and river discharge to the sea.

items.stem: Ana writes: "Infiltration and percolation are the same process." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Infiltration is water entering the soil; percolation is deeper movement into rock.
items.markingKey: Infiltration is water entering the soil; percolation is deeper movement into rock. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between infiltration and percolation.
items.answer: Infiltration is the movement of water from the surface into the soil; percolation is the deeper movement from the soil into permeable rock to become groundwater.
items.markingKey: Infiltration is the movement of water from the surface into the soil; percolation is the deeper movement from the soil into permeable rock to become groundwater. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: The following channel depths (cm) measured across the River Ilz were recorded: 6, 55, 71, 22, 11, 40, 5, 63, 45. Calculate the mean, median and range.
items.answer: mean 35.3; median 40; range 66
items.markingKey: A1 mean 35.3; A1 median 40 (data ordered); A1 range 66.

items.stem: Between 1995 and 2015 the groundwater level below the surface at a well near Mexico City changed from 75.8 to 133.9 m. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (133.9 − 75.8) ÷ 75.8 × 100; A1 +76.6% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: A storm hydrograph for an urban stream in Hamburg shows peak rainfall at 03:00 on day 1 and peak discharge 7 hours later. Discharge rose from a baseflow of 5.0 m³/s to a peak of 19.5 m³/s. (a) Calculate the lag time and the increase in discharge above baseflow. (b) Describe the shape of the hydrograph and suggest two catchment characteristics that explain it.
items.answer: (a) 7 h; 14.5 m³/s above baseflow (b) flashy (short lag, steep rising limb); e.g. impermeable urban surfaces, steep slopes, thin soils, high drainage density
items.markingKey: (a) A1 7 h, A1 14.5 m³/s. (b) R1 shape, R1 R1 two linked catchment factors.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that human activity now has a greater influence on drainage basin systems than physical factors?
items.answer: Human activity dominates in heavily used basins, but physical factors still set the framework.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: urbanisation, deforestation and dams alter flows (Amazon, Yangtze); irrigation and abstraction remove large volumes. Against / limitations: climate, geology and relief remain the basic controls; many remote basins are little modified. A supported conclusion might be: Human activity dominates in heavily used basins, but physical factors still set the framework. items.stem: Explain how urbanisation changes drainage basin flows.
items.answer: Impermeable surfaces reduce infiltration and storage, increasing overland flow; drains speed water to channels; less evapotranspiration; so runoff is greater and faster.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Impermeable surfaces reduce infiltration and storage, increasing overland flow; drains speed water to channels; less evapotranspiration; so runoff is greater and faster. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between overland flow and throughflow.
items.answer: Throughflow is the slow lateral movement of water within the soil; overland flow is the rapid movement of water across the ground surface when the soil cannot absorb more.
items.markingKey: Throughflow is the slow lateral movement of water within the soil; overland flow is the rapid movement of water across the ground surface when the soil cannot absorb more. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A basin receives 900 mm of precipitation a year; evapotranspiration is 450 mm and there is no change in storage. Calculate the annual runoff and explain the result.
items.answer: Q = P − E = 900 − 450 = 450 mm; half of the precipitation leaves as river discharge, typical of a temperate humid basin.
items.markingKey: Q = P − E = 900 − 450 = 450 mm; half of the precipitation leaves as river discharge, typical of a temperate humid basin.

items.stem: In August 2004, Boscastle in Cornwall flooded after about how much rain fell in about five hours?
items.answer: About 200 mm
items.markingKey: About 200 mm. The small, steep Valency catchment produced a flash flood; around 100 people were rescued by helicopter.

items.stem: A student claims: "Lag time is measured from the start of rainfall to the peak discharge." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Lag time is measured from peak rainfall to peak discharge.
items.markingKey: Lag time is measured from peak rainfall to peak discharge. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain how antecedent moisture affects the shape of a storm hydrograph.
items.answer: If soil is already saturated from earlier rain, infiltration is low, so more rain becomes overland flow, giving a shorter lag time and higher peak. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If soil is already saturated from earlier rain, infiltration is low, so more rain becomes overland flow, giving a shorter lag time and higher peak. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Annual maximum discharges (m³/s) recorded for the River Ouse at York over 10 years (1996-2005), ranked from highest: 2269, 2171, 2059, 1849, 1625, 1359, 1156, 1009, 736, 239. Calculate the recurrence interval of the flood ranked 5 (1625 m³/s) using RI = (n + 1)/m, and its annual probability.
items.answer: RI = (10 + 1)/5 = 2.2 years; probability ≈ 45.5% in any year

items.stem:
Study the resource below.

Table: lag times for two catchments after the same storm - Catchment A (urban, 65% impermeable): 2.5 h, peak 28 m³/s; Catchment B (forested, 5% impermeable): 11 h, peak 9 m³/s.

Explain the differences shown.
items.answer: Impermeable surfaces and drains in A cause rapid overland flow; in B interception, infiltration and throughflow delay and reduce runoff.
items.markingKey: Impermeable surfaces and drains in A cause rapid overland flow; in B interception, infiltration and throughflow delay and reduce runoff. Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Hydrograph data: rainfall peaked at 10:00 (25 mm/h); discharge rose from a baseflow of 4 m³/s at 09:00 to a peak of 38 m³/s at 16:00, returning to 6 m³/s by 08:00 the next day.

(a) Calculate the lag time and the peak storm flow above baseflow. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, suggest why discharge did not return fully to its original baseflow. [6]
items.answer: (a) Lag time = 16:00 − 10:00 = 6 hours; 38 − 4 = 34 m³/s above baseflow. (b) Groundwater and throughflow recharged by the storm continue to feed the channel, raising baseflow for a time.
items.markingKey: (a) Lag time = 16:00 − 10:00 = 6 hours; 38 − 4 = 34 m³/s above baseflow. (b) Groundwater and throughflow recharged by the storm continue to feed the channel, raising baseflow for a time. Credit relevant own knowledge and named examples in (b). items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The total length of river channels in a basin divided by its area (km/km²)"?
items.answer: drainage density
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of drainage density.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "abrasion"?
options: A sinuous bend in a river channel, with erosion on the outer bank and deposition on the inner bank
The capture of precipitation by vegetation before it reaches the ground
The boundary of a drainage basin, usually a ridge of high land
Erosion caused when the river's load scrapes and wears away the bed and banks (also called corrasion)
items.answer: Erosion caused when the river's load scrapes and wears away the bed and banks (also called corrasion)
items.markingKey: D. "abrasion" is erosion caused when the river's load scrapes and wears away the bed and banks (also called corrasion).

items.stem: Explain the formation of a meander.
items.answer: Riffles and pools develop; helicoidal flow concentrates the fastest flow towards the outer bank, causing erosion (river cliff), while slower flow on the inner bank deposits sediment (point bar); the bend migrates and becomes more sinuous.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Riffles and pools develop; helicoidal flow concentrates the fastest flow towards the outer bank, causing erosion (river cliff), while slower flow on the inner bank deposits sediment (point bar); the bend migrates and becomes more sinuous. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between traction and suspension.
items.answer: Suspension carries fine particles (clay, silt) within the water; traction rolls large boulders and cobbles along the bed.
items.markingKey: Suspension carries fine particles (clay, silt) within the water; traction rolls large boulders and cobbles along the bed. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: The following slope angles (°) along a hillslope profile in Yunnan were recorded: 35, 31, 11, 19, 33, 14, 10, 8, 15. Calculate the mean, median and range.
items.answer: mean 19.6; median 15; range 27
items.markingKey: A1 mean 19.6; A1 median 15 (data ordered); A1 range 27.

items.stem: With reference to the Rakaia River, New Zealand, explain how it illustrates braiding.
items.answer: A braided river crossing the Canterbury Plains with many channels separated by gravel bars. High loads of coarse sediment and variable discharge from glacial meltwater produce multiple channels.
items.markingKey: Context (A braided river crossing the Canterbury Plains with many channels separated by gravel bars.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: High loads of coarse sediment and variable discharge from glacial meltwater produce multiple channels. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to braiding.

items.stem: Briefly analyse two contrasting points of view on the statement: "Deposition is more important than erosion in creating river landforms."
items.answer: Both processes are important; many landforms, such as meanders, result from their interaction.
items.markingKey: For: floodplains, levées, point bars, deltas are depositional. Against: waterfalls, gorges, V-shaped valleys and river cliffs are erosional. [4]: 1 mark for a valid argument for, 1 for its development; 1 mark for a valid argument against, 1 for its development; generic points without geographical context are capped at 2.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "abrasion".
items.answer: Erosion caused when the river's load scrapes and wears away the bed and banks (also called corrasion)

items.stem:
The table shows data for sites on a stream in Snowdonia (site: distance downstream (km), mean pebble long axis (mm)).
A: 7.9, 137; B: 7.6, 138; C: 14.3, 44; D: 10.2, 65; E: 15.8, 54; F: 3.8, 141.
Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (rs = 1 − 6Σd² / (n³ − n)) and state whether the relationship is significant at the 0.05 level (one-tailed test; critical value for n = 6: 0.829).
items.answer: Σd² = 68; rs = 1 − 6×68/(6³ − 6) = -0.943; a negative correlation that is significant at the 0.05 level.
items.markingKey: M1 ranking both variables (rank 1 = highest); M1 d² summed: Σd² = 68; A1 rs = -0.943; R1 |rs| >= 0.829 so reject the null hypothesis.

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Cross-section description: at a meander bend, depth is 0.2 m at the inner bank, 0.5 m mid-channel and 1.3 m at the outer bank; velocity is 0.3 m/s near the inner bank and 1.1 m/s near the outer bank.

(a) Describe the asymmetry of the cross-section. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, explain the asymmetry using the velocity data. [6]
items.answer: (a) Shallow, gently sloping inner bank (point bar) and deep, steep outer bank (river cliff); depth increases from 0.2 to 1.3 m. (b) Faster flow (1.1 m/s) on the outer bank erodes it by hydraulic action and abrasion; slower flow (0.3 m/s) on the inner bank causes deposition.
items.markingKey: (a) Shallow, gently sloping inner bank (point bar) and deep, steep outer bank (river cliff); depth increases from 0.2 to 1.3 m. (b) Faster flow (1.1 m/s) on the outer bank erodes it by hydraulic action and abrasion; slower flow (0.3 m/s) on the inner bank causes deposition. Credit relevant own knowledge and named examples in (b). items.stem: What was the approximate cost of the 2011 floods in Thailand, which affected Bangkok and its industrial estates?
items.answer: About US$45 billion
items.markingKey: About US$45 billion. The World Bank estimated about US$46.5 billion of damage and losses; global electronics and car supply chains were disrupted.

items.stem: Explain how deforestation upstream can increase flooding downstream.
items.answer: Reduced interception and infiltration increase overland flow; soil erosion adds sediment that reduces channel capacity, e.g. debated links between Himalayan deforestation and Ganges-Brahmaputra floods.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Reduced interception and infiltration increase overland flow; soil erosion adds sediment that reduces channel capacity, e.g. debated links between Himalayan deforestation and Ganges-Brahmaputra floods. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Flood defences make floodplains completely safe." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Defences are designed for a given recurrence interval (e.g. 1 in 100 years) and can be exceeded or fail, as New Orleans levees did in 2005.
items.markingKey: Defences are designed for a given recurrence interval (e.g. 1 in 100 years) and can be exceeded or fail, as New Orleans levees did in 2005. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (362 − 558) ÷ 558 × 100; A1 -35.1% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Room for the River programme, Netherlands shows soft flood management.
items.answer: Over 30 projects on the Rhine branches (2006-2015) cost about €2.3 billion. Giving the river space lowered flood levels while improving landscape and habitats.
items.markingKey: Context (Over 30 projects on the Rhine branches (2006-2015) cost about €2.3 billion.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Using a named example, outline two consequences of a river flood.
items.answer: e.g. 2011 Thailand floods: over 800 deaths and 13 million people affected; industrial estates north of Bangkok flooded, disrupting global hard-disk and car supply chains (about US$45 billion losses).
items.markingKey: e.g. 2011 Thailand floods: over 800 deaths and 13 million people affected; industrial estates north of Bangkok flooded, disrupting global hard-disk and car supply chains (about US$45 billion losses).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that soft engineering is more effective than hard engineering in managing flood risk.
items.answer: A combination is most effective; soft engineering is preferable where land is available, hard engineering where high-value assets must be protected.

items.stem: Explain why soft engineering is increasingly preferred to hard engineering.
items.answer: It is cheaper to maintain, works with natural processes, provides habitat and amenity, reduces downstream impacts and is more resilient to climate change.

items.stem: Explain the difference between soft engineering and hard engineering.
items.answer: Hard engineering controls rivers with structures such as dams, levées and channelisation; soft engineering works with natural processes through zoning, afforestation, wetland restoration and warnings.
items.markingKey: Hard engineering controls rivers with structures such as dams, levées and channelisation; soft engineering works with natural processes through zoning, afforestation, wetland restoration and warnings. items.stem: Define the term "drainage basin".
items.answer: An area of land drained by a river and its tributaries, separated from neighbouring basins by a watershed

items.stem: Which basin characteristic tends to produce the shortest lag time?
options: Small, steep basin with impermeable rock and high drainage density
items.answer: Small, steep basin with impermeable rock and high drainage density
items.markingKey: C. Water reaches the channel quickly by overland flow.

items.stem: "Rivers erode most in their upper course because they flow fastest there." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Velocity often increases downstream as channel efficiency improves; upper courses erode vertically because of steep gradients and coarse load.
items.markingKey: Velocity often increases downstream as channel efficiency improves; upper courses erode vertically because of steep gradients and coarse load. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Groundwater flow is the fastest route for water to reach a river." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Groundwater flow is the slowest route (days to years); overland flow is fastest.
items.markingKey: Groundwater flow is the slowest route (days to years); overland flow is fastest. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Floods are entirely negative." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Floods deposit fertile silt, recharge groundwater and wetlands and support floodplain agriculture, e.g. in Bangladesh.
items.markingKey: Floods deposit fertile silt, recharge groundwater and wetlands and support floodplain agriculture, e.g. in Bangladesh. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between baseflow and storm flow.
items.answer: Baseflow is the steady contribution from groundwater; storm flow (quickflow) is the extra discharge from overland flow and rapid throughflow after rainfall.
items.markingKey: Baseflow is the steady contribution from groundwater; storm flow (quickflow) is the extra discharge from overland flow and rapid throughflow after rainfall. items.stem: Explain why particle size usually decreases downstream.
items.answer: Attrition and abrasion wear particles down during transport, and selective transport carries finer material further while coarse material is deposited upstream.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Attrition and abrasion wear particles down during transport, and selective transport carries finer material further while coarse material is deposited upstream. items.stem: Briefly explain why the drainage basin is described as an open system.
items.answer: It receives inputs of energy (solar) and matter (precipitation) from outside and loses outputs (evapotranspiration, river discharge to the sea), with stores and flows inside the system.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It receives inputs of energy (solar) and matter (precipitation) from outside and loses outputs (evapotranspiration, river discharge to the sea), with stores and flows inside the system. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

Describe the asymmetry of the cross-section.
items.answer: Shallow, gently sloping inner bank (point bar) and deep, steep outer bank (river cliff); depth increases from 0.2 to 1.3 m.
items.markingKey: Shallow, gently sloping inner bank (point bar) and deep, steep outer bank (river cliff); depth increases from 0.2 to 1.3 m. Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Systems diagram description: precipitation → interception storage → throughfall/stemflow → surface storage → infiltration → soil water → percolation → groundwater; flows out via overland flow, throughflow and groundwater flow to channel; outputs: evaporation, transpiration, channel discharge.

(a) Identify two stores and two flows shown. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, explain what happens to flows when the soil becomes saturated. [6]
items.answer: (a) Stores: interception, surface, soil water, groundwater, channel. Flows: throughfall, stemflow, infiltration, percolation, throughflow, overland flow, groundwater flow. (b) Infiltration falls to zero, so additional rain becomes saturation-excess overland flow, raising and speeding river discharge.
items.markingKey: (a) Stores: interception, surface, soil water, groundwater, channel. Flows: throughfall, stemflow, infiltration, percolation, throughflow, overland flow, groundwater flow. items.stem: To what extent is it true that soft engineering is more effective than hard engineering in managing flood risk? Refer to places and scales you have studied.
items.answer: A combination is most effective; soft engineering is preferable where land is available, hard engineering where high-value assets must be protected.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: works with natural processes, lower maintenance, sustainable (Room for the River); avoids the levée effect and downstream impacts. Arguments challenging it: dense cities need hard defences (Thames Barrier, Three Gorges); soft measures need land and time. Evaluation should weigh places, scales, perspectives and time. Judgement: A combination is most effective; soft engineering is preferable where land is available, hard engineering where high-value assets must be protected. items.stem: "Deposition is more important than erosion in creating river landforms." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Both processes are important; many landforms, such as meanders, result from their interaction.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: floodplains, levées, point bars, deltas are depositional; lowland rivers deposit most of their load. Arguments challenging it: waterfalls, gorges, V-shaped valleys and river cliffs are erosional; meanders depend on both erosion and deposition. Evaluation should weigh places, scales, perspectives and time. Judgement: Both processes are important; many landforms, such as meanders, result from their interaction. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An area of land drained by a river and its tributaries, separated from neighbouring basins by a watershed"?
items.answer: drainage basin
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of drainage basin.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "recurrence interval".
items.answer: The average time between floods of a given magnitude, calculated as (n + 1)/m from ranked records
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the average time between floods of a given magnitude, calculated as (n + 1)/m from ranked records. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "rising limb".
items.answer: The part of a hydrograph showing the increase in discharge after rainfall begins
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the part of a hydrograph showing the increase in discharge after rainfall begins. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Tariq writes: "Rivers erode most in their upper course because they flow fastest there." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Velocity often increases downstream as channel efficiency improves; upper courses erode vertically because of steep gradients and coarse load.
items.markingKey: Velocity often increases downstream as channel efficiency improves; upper courses erode vertically because of steep gradients and coarse load. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how vegetation affects the drainage basin hydrological cycle.
items.answer: Interception stores water on leaves and increases evaporation; roots increase infiltration; transpiration returns water to the atmosphere; leaf litter slows overland flow - so forested basins have lower and slower runoff.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Interception stores water on leaves and increases evaporation; roots increase infiltration; transpiration returns water to the atmosphere; leaf litter slows overland flow - so forested basins have lower and slower runoff. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between flood prediction and flood prevention.
items.answer: Prediction forecasts when and where floods will occur so people can prepare; prevention attempts to stop floods happening by controlling discharge or channel capacity.
items.markingKey: Prediction forecasts when and where floods will occur so people can prepare; prevention attempts to stop floods happening by controlling discharge or channel capacity. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a subdued hydrograph and a flashy hydrograph.
items.answer: A flashy hydrograph has a short lag time, steep rising limb and high peak (urban, steep, impermeable basins); a subdued hydrograph has a long lag, gentle limbs and lower peak (forested, permeable, gentle basins).
items.markingKey: A flashy hydrograph has a short lag time, steep rising limb and high peak (urban, steep, impermeable basins); a subdued hydrograph has a long lag, gentle limbs and lower peak (forested, permeable, gentle basins). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a river cliff and a point bar.
items.answer: A river cliff is a steep erosional bank on the outside of a meander; a point bar is a gentle depositional slope of sand and gravel on the inside.
items.markingKey: A river cliff is a steep erosional bank on the outside of a meander; a point bar is a gentle depositional slope of sand and gravel on the inside. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between throughflow and overland flow.
items.answer: Throughflow is the slow lateral movement of water within the soil; overland flow is the rapid movement of water across the ground surface when the soil cannot absorb more.
items.markingKey: Throughflow is the slow lateral movement of water within the soil; overland flow is the rapid movement of water across the ground surface when the soil cannot absorb more. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A storm hydrograph for a small urban catchment in Kuala Lumpur shows peak rainfall at 08:00 on day 1 and peak discharge 4 hours later. Discharge rose from a baseflow of 20.0 m³/s to a peak of 117.6 m³/s. State the time of peak discharge and the lag time.
items.answer: Peak at 12:00 on day 1; lag time 4 hours
items.markingKey: A1 12:00 day 1; A1 lag time 4 h (time from peak rainfall to peak discharge).

items.stem: Using the Boscastle flood (2004) as an example, explain factors influencing the storm hydrograph.
items.answer: About 200 mm of rain in roughly five hours on the steep, small Valency catchment produced a flash flood that destroyed cars and buildings. Intense rainfall on a small, steep basin with saturated soils produced a very short lag time.
items.markingKey: Context (About 200 mm of rain in roughly five hours on the steep, small Valency catchment produced a flash flood that destroyed cars and buildings.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Intense rainfall on a small, steep basin with saturated soils produced a very short lag time. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to factors influencing the storm hydrograph.

items.stem: Suggest two field measurements that could test whether pebble size decreases downstream.
